name: On the Origin of Species
info: On the Origin of Species is a book by the English naturalist Charles Darwin, published in London on 24 November 1859, which set out evolution by natural selection and common descent and became the foundation of evolutionary biology.

facts.made: Charles Darwin, English naturalist, who drew on his Beagle voyage of the 1830s and on years of research, correspondence and experiment; published by John Murray
facts.form: A work of scientific literature in prose, written for non-specialist readers as an abstract of a larger planned work; twelve chapters in the manuscript Darwin described to his publisher in 1859, revised through six editions
facts.where: Read in printed editions and translations; all six British editions are available at The Complete Works of Charles Darwin Online
facts.known: Natural selection; the struggle for existence; common descent and the tree of life; the closing passage on the entangled bank; the pigeon breeding analogy; the phrase survival of the fittest, added in the fifth edition

t: Darwin argued that species were not separately created but arose by common descent in a branching pattern, with natural selection as the chief agent of change.
The book was an abstract hurried into print after Alfred Russel Wallace sent Darwin an essay describing a similar mechanism, and it went through six editions in Darwin's lifetime.
Within two decades most scientists accepted evolution, but natural selection became central to evolutionary theory only with the modern evolutionary synthesis of the 1930s and 1940s.
dyk: The first printing of 1250 copies was offered to booksellers on 22 November 1859, and all available copies were taken up at once; Mudie's Library alone took 500.
ev: Darwin reads Thomas Malthus on population and sees how selection among varieties could work in nature
Darwin expands his sketch of his theory into a 230-page Essay, to be published if he died prematurely
Papers by Wallace and Darwin are read at the Linnean Society, and Darwin begins his abstract on 20 July
On the Origin of Species is published by John Murray on 24 November
The second edition adds the phrase by the Creator to the closing sentence, and Appleton's issues the American edition
The sixth edition appears as The Origin of Species at half the price, after Darwin answers George Jackson Mivart
The modern evolutionary synthesis makes natural selection central to evolutionary theory

sections.origins:
Evolutionary ideas existed before Darwin. In the 1790s his grandfather Erasmus Darwin outlined a hypothesis of the transmutation of species, and in 1809 Jean-Baptiste Lamarck published a more developed theory in which organisms adapted by inheriting changes caused by use or disuse. Such ideas were controversial because they conflicted with the beliefs that species were unchanging parts of a designed hierarchy and that humans were unique. In the first half of the 19th century the English scientific establishment was closely tied to the Church of England, and science was part of natural theology.

Darwin studied medicine at Edinburgh from 1825, then learnt science as natural theology at Cambridge. In December 1831 he joined the Beagle expedition as a gentleman naturalist and geologist, and in March 1837 the ornithologist John Gould told him that mockingbirds from the Galápagos Islands represented three separate species. Darwin began to speculate in notebooks that one species might change into another. In late September 1838 he read Malthus, and by December he had noted a similarity between breeders selecting traits and nature selecting among variants.
sections.content:
The book argues that species had not been separately created and that natural selection had been the chief agent of change. Ernst Mayr later summarised the argument as facts and inferences: species are fertile enough that populations would grow if all offspring survived, yet populations stay roughly stable; resources are limited, so a struggle for survival follows; individuals vary and much of the variation is heritable; those better suited to the environment leave more offspring. The accumulation of such variations produces new species.

The first four chapters compare selection in nature with the selection practised by breeders, using fancy pigeons, all descended from the rock dove, as the main illustration. Later chapters take up difficulties for the theory, including the rarity of transitional forms, the origin of complex organs such as the eye, instincts such as the cell-building of honey bees, and the imperfection of the geological record. Further chapters set out evidence from the distribution of species, from classification, from homologous structures such as the hand of a man and the wing of a bat, from embryos and from rudimentary organs. The final chapter ends with the passage on an entangled bank and a single sentence saying that light will be thrown on the origin of man and his history.
sections.making:
Darwin had the framework of his theory by 1838 but published it only in 1859. He roughed out a 35-page Pencil Sketch in June 1842 and a 230-page Essay by July 1844, then spent eight years on barnacles and began working full time on evolution in 1854. By 1856 his theory had a mass of supporting evidence. In May 1856, after Charles Lyell urged him to publish to establish priority, he began a sketch that grew into a planned big book on Natural Selection. Biographers have proposed various personal reasons for the delay, while the historian John van Wyhe has found that the idea of a delay dates only from the 1940s.

On 18 June 1858 Darwin received from Alfred Russel Wallace, then in the Maluku Islands, twenty pages describing a mechanism similar to his own. Lyell and Joseph Dalton Hooker arranged a joint presentation at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858, which drew little reaction. Darwin then began an abstract of his whole work on 20 July. John Murray agreed in March 1859 to publish it on the terms he gave Lyell, and objected to the word abstract in the title. After a draft title suggested On the Mutability of Species, the title was settled with Murray's persuasion as On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection.
sections.reception:
The book was written for non-specialist readers and attracted widespread interest. Much of the early reaction was hostile, in large part because few reviewers understood the theory, but Darwin was already respected as a scientist and had to be taken seriously. Samuel Wilberforce disagreed with the argument in the Quarterly Review in 1860. Human origins became central to the debate, although Darwin had avoided the subject in the book, and Thomas Henry Huxley argued it strongly. Huxley used the debate to promote scientific naturalism over natural theology, and the X Club shaped much late-Victorian science.

By 1875 most scientists accepted that evolution occurred, but few thought natural selection significant. Objections included William Thomson's calculation that the Sun was only about 100 million years old and Fleeming Jenkin's argument that blending inheritance would prevent useful traits from accumulating. From the 1880s to the 1930s, in what is called the eclipse of Darwinism, saltationism, orthogenesis and neo-Lamarckism were given more credit. Religious responses ranged widely. Charles Kingsley saw natural selection as a noble conception of the Deity, Asa Gray defended the book in terms of theistic evolution, and Charles Hodge argued in 1874 that Darwinism, defined as rejecting design, was atheism. Political commentators also drew on the book, among them Herbert Spencer, whom Darwin credited with the phrase survival of the fittest.
sections.survival:
Darwin revised the text through six editions. The second, of 3,000 copies, appeared on 7 January 1860 with a new epigraph from Charles Kingsley and the phrase by the Creator in the last sentence. The third edition of 1861 added An Historical Sketch of the Recent Progress of Opinion on the Origin of Species, in which Darwin acknowledged that Patrick Matthew had anticipated natural selection in 1831. The fifth edition of 10 February 1869 first used survival of the fittest. The sixth, of 19 February 1872, answered George Jackson Mivart's objections in a new chapter, used the word evolution for the first time, dropped On from the title and was priced at 7s 6d. Darwin had been told of working men in Lancashire clubbing together to buy the fifth edition.

Translations spread the book, but some carried their translators' own ideas. Heinrich Georg Bronn's German version of 1860 added essays and rendered favoured races as perfected races, and Clémence Royer's French version of 1862 added an introduction and notes that troubled Darwin. He remained unsatisfied until Edmond Barbier's translation of 1876. By Darwin's death in 1882 the book was in its sixth edition. A variorum recording every change between the editions was first published in 1959 and a concordance in 1981.
sections.legacy:
The book legitimised scientific discussion of evolutionary mechanisms, and the new term Darwinism was used for the whole range of evolutionism. It was given more popular attention than almost any other scientific work. With the modern evolutionary synthesis of the 1930s and 1940s, when R. A. Fisher, Sewall Wright and J. B. S. Haldane merged Darwinian selection with a statistical understanding of Mendelian genetics, natural selection became central to evolutionary theory. Darwin's theory, with its tree-like model of branching common descent, has become the unifying theory of the life sciences, and it has become essential to applied sciences such as medicine and agriculture.

Darwin followed the book with The Variation of Animals and Plants Under Domestication in 1868 and The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex in 1871, in which he published his own views on human evolution. Scholars have produced an extensive literature on his life and work, called the Darwin Industry. The book also lies behind a religion-based political controversy over how evolution is taught in schools, especially in the United States, where the American creation–evolution controversy began in the 1920s.

summary: On the Origin of Species is Charles Darwin's book of 1859 arguing that species arose by common descent through natural selection. Written as an abstract after Wallace's essay reached him, it went through six editions and became the foundation of evolutionary biology.

notes: The article says the manuscript headings Darwin listed to Murray on 31 March 1859 were 12 chapters in progress; the published book's chapter count is not stated, so 'form' speaks only of the manuscript.
The article's text mentions the first edition's chapter VII (instincts) and a new chapter VII added in the sixth edition; chapters are not numbered in the profile for that reason.
Darwin is said to have read Malthus in late September 1838; the 1838 event uses that date. The article gives Gould's announcement as March 1837.

Left out: the Oxford evolution debate details beyond the Huxley and Owen dispute, the Hippocampus Question, impact in Russia, Germany and America, and the 2009 commemorations; the first printing details are as the article gives them (1250 printed, about 1,170 available for sale).
'Praise words' in quotations are not used. The Academic Book Week survey is reported as the article reports it; the editor may drop it as a ranking.
The 1930s event uses the article's 'the 1930s and 1940s'. The 1860 American edition: the article says Appleton's got their edition out in mid-January 1860.
